project.title: The Odyssey Storybook
project.violenceGuidance: Allow suspense and scary moments, avoid gore.
project.structure: Modular scenes for iterative web story cards.

fleetStates.label: Leaving Troy
fleetStates.note: Homer states that Odysseus has twelve ships; the man count is a visual estimate using about fifty men per ship.

fleetStates.label: After the Cicones
fleetStates.certainty: ships exact, losses exact, men estimated
fleetStates.note: The poem says six men from each of twelve ships died at Ismarus: seventy-two total.

fleetStates.label: After the Lotus-Eaters
fleetStates.note: No deaths are reported among the Lotus-Eaters; the danger is forgetting home.

fleetStates.label: After Polyphemus
fleetStates.certainty: ships exact, losses exact, men estimated
fleetStates.note: Odysseus takes twelve selected men into the cave; six companions are killed before the escape.

fleetStates.label: After Aeolus
fleetStates.note: No deaths are reported at Aeolia, but the fleet loses its near-return to Ithaca.

fleetStates.label: After the Laestrygonians
fleetStates.note: Only Odysseus' ship escapes. The later Circe episode implies a small crew, split into two groups, one led by Eurylochus with twenty-two men.

fleetStates.label: After Circe
fleetStates.note: Elpenor dies at Circe's house before the underworld journey; Homer does not give a full surviving roster.

fleetStates.label: After Scylla
fleetStates.note: Scylla takes six men from the final ship.

fleetStates.label: After Zeus' Storm
fleetStates.note: Zeus destroys the last ship after the cattle of Helios are killed; Odysseus alone reaches Ogygia.

fleetStates.label: Odysseus Alone
fleetStates.note: The crew story is over; the return now depends on Odysseus, divine help, and Phaeacian hospitality.

journeySequence.label: Troy
journeySequence.event: Odysseus leaves Troy after the long war.
journeySequence.sequenceNote: Backstory node; useful if we later add a short prologue.

journeySequence.label: Land of the Cicones
journeySequence.event: The crew raids Ismarus and suffers an early loss.
journeySequence.sequenceNote: Now tracked as the first full travel scene after Troy.

journeySequence.label: The Lotus-Eaters
journeySequence.event: Some sailors eat the lotus and forget the wish to go home.

journeySequence.label: The Cyclops' Cave
journeySequence.event: Odysseus blinds Polyphemus and brings Poseidon's anger.
journeySequence.sequenceNote: Major turning point: cleverness works, pride costs him.

journeySequence.label: Aeolia
journeySequence.event: Aeolus gives the bag of winds, but the crew opens it near Ithaca.
journeySequence.sequenceNote: They nearly reach home, then lose it.

journeySequence.label: The Laestrygonians
journeySequence.event: Giant Laestrygonians destroy all but Odysseus' ship.
journeySequence.sequenceNote: The journey narrows from a fleet to one ship.

journeySequence.label: Aeaea
journeySequence.event: Circe transforms some of the crew, then becomes an uneasy helper.

journeySequence.label: The Underworld
journeySequence.event: Odysseus seeks Tiresias and receives warnings about the road home.
journeySequence.sequenceNote: A spiritual journey rather than ordinary geography.

journeySequence.label: Return to Aeaea
journeySequence.event: Odysseus returns to Circe, who explains the next dangers.
journeySequence.sequenceNote: Repeated node on purpose: the route returns to Circe before moving on.

journeySequence.label: The Sirens
journeySequence.event: The crew rows past the deadly song while Odysseus is tied to the mast.
journeySequence.sequenceNote: Self-control and curiosity meet real danger.

journeySequence.label: Scylla and Charybdis
journeySequence.event: Odysseus chooses the monster over the whirlpool and loses more men.

journeySequence.label: Thrinacia
journeySequence.event: The hungry crew kills the sacred cattle of the Sun.

journeySequence.label: The Last Shipwreck
journeySequence.event: Zeus destroys the ship, and Odysseus alone survives.
journeySequence.sequenceNote: Connective route node explaining why Odysseus reaches Calypso alone.

journeySequence.label: Ogygia
journeySequence.event: Calypso keeps Odysseus on her island for years.
journeySequence.sequenceNote: Chronologically this follows the shipwreck, even though Homer reveals it early.

journeySequence.label: Scheria Shore
journeySequence.event: Poseidon's storm wrecks the raft, and Odysseus reaches Scheria.
journeySequence.sequenceNote: Final survival test before Odysseus tells his story.

journeySequence.label: Phaeacian Palace
journeySequence.event: The Phaeacians welcome Odysseus and agree to send him home.
journeySequence.sequenceNote: This is where many earlier stops are narrated as flashback in Homer.

journeySequence.label: Eumaeus' Hut
journeySequence.event: Odysseus reaches Ithaca in disguise and tests loyalty.
journeySequence.sequenceNote: The homecoming begins quietly, before the palace reveal.

journeySequence.label: Ithaca Palace
journeySequence.event: Odysseus returns to the palace, strings the bow, and reunites with Penelope.
journeySequence.sequenceNote: The route ends at home, but the household still has to be restored.

journeySequence.label: Ithaca Countryside
journeySequence.event: The last threat of violence is stopped, and peace returns.
journeySequence.sequenceNote: Ending node: home becomes whole again.

storyOutlineOrder.timelineNote: The first stop after Troy shows Odysseus' men winning, lingering too long, and paying for it.
Odysseus' early wanderings after leaving Troy.
Before Poseidon's curse fully shapes the journey.
The crew nearly reaches Ithaca, then loses the chance.
The fleet is reduced to Odysseus' single ship.
Circe delays the crew, then sends Odysseus toward prophecy.
Odysseus receives warnings about the road ahead.
The Sirens come first, then the impossible passage.
The final ship is lost after the sacred cattle are harmed.
Odysseus is stranded with Calypso after the last shipwreck.
Meanwhile, Ithaca has been under pressure for years.
Athena starts the Ithaca thread moving while Odysseus' return nears.
Telemachus searches for news of Odysseus.
Telemachus gains hope while the suitors become more dangerous.
Odysseus leaves Ogygia and survives Poseidon's storm.
The Phaeacians hear Odysseus' story and send him home.
Odysseus reaches Ithaca but must stay hidden.
Telemachus returns and learns his father is alive.
Odysseus tests the palace while disguised.
Penelope's bow contest reveals who still has Odysseus' strength.
Odysseus reveals himself and ends the suitors' rule.
Penelope proves the truth through the secret of the marriage bed.
The final threat is stopped and Ithaca becomes whole again.

scenes.title: The Cicones
scenes.summary: After leaving Troy, Odysseus and his men raid the Cicones, linger too long, and are driven back to sea with painful losses.

scenes.title: Trouble in Ithaca
scenes.summary: Penelope and Telemachus struggle while suitors crowd Odysseus' palace.

scenes.title: Athena Sends Telemachus Out
scenes.summary: Athena gives Telemachus courage and urges him to search for news of his father.

scenes.title: Telemachus Visits Nestor
scenes.summary: Telemachus visits Pylos and hears memories of the Greek heroes after Troy.

scenes.title: Telemachus Visits Menelaus and Helen
scenes.summary: In Sparta, Telemachus learns that Odysseus may still be alive.

scenes.title: Odysseus on Calypso's Island
scenes.summary: Odysseus longs for home on Calypso's island until the gods order his release.

scenes.title: The Storm and the Phaeacian Shore
scenes.summary: Poseidon wrecks Odysseus' raft, but Odysseus survives and reaches Scheria.

scenes.title: Nausicaa and the Phaeacian Court
scenes.summary: Nausicaa and the Phaeacians welcome Odysseus, who begins to reveal his grief.

scenes.title: The Lotus-Eaters
scenes.summary: Some sailors eat lotus flowers and forget they ever wanted to go home.

scenes.title: The Cyclops' Cave
scenes.summary: Odysseus tricks Polyphemus and escapes, but pride brings Poseidon's curse.

scenes.title: Aeolus and the Bag of Winds
scenes.summary: The crew opens Aeolus' wind bag just as Ithaca is nearly in sight.

scenes.title: The Laestrygonians
scenes.summary: Giant Laestrygonians attack, and only Odysseus' ship escapes.

scenes.title: Circe's Island
scenes.summary: Circe transforms some men, then becomes an uneasy helper to Odysseus.

scenes.title: The Underworld
scenes.summary: Odysseus visits the dead and receives a warning from Tiresias.

scenes.title: Sirens, Scylla, and Charybdis
scenes.summary: Odysseus faces the Sirens' song and the terrible passage between monster and whirlpool.

scenes.title: The Cattle of the Sun
scenes.summary: The hungry crew disobeys the warning and harms Helios' sacred cattle.

scenes.title: Home to Ithaca in Disguise
scenes.summary: Odysseus returns to Ithaca disguised as an old beggar and visits Eumaeus.

scenes.title: Father and Son
scenes.summary: Odysseus reveals himself to Telemachus, and they plan together.

scenes.title: The Beggar in the Palace
scenes.summary: Odysseus enters his palace in disguise and sees the suitors' behavior.

scenes.title: The Bow Contest
scenes.summary: Penelope sets the contest of Odysseus' bow, and the disguised Odysseus succeeds.

scenes.title: The Reckoning
scenes.summary: Odysseus reveals himself and defeats the suitors with help from loyal allies.

scenes.title: Penelope's Test
scenes.summary: Penelope tests Odysseus with the secret of their olive-tree bed.

scenes.title: Peace in Ithaca
scenes.summary: After one last threat of violence, Athena helps restore peace in Ithaca.

glossaryEntries.title: Odysseus
glossaryEntries.text: King of Ithaca: brilliant, brave, proud, tricky, loving, and complicated.

glossaryEntries.title: Penelope
glossaryEntries.text: Odysseus' wife and Telemachus' mother. She survives by patience, intelligence, and careful tests instead of force.

glossaryEntries.title: Telemachus
glossaryEntries.text: The son of Odysseus and Penelope. His arc is learning how to become brave before he knows whether his father is alive.

glossaryEntries.title: Athena
glossaryEntries.text: Goddess of wisdom, strategy, and courageous action. She helps Odysseus and Telemachus, often through disguise.

glossaryEntries.title: Poseidon
glossaryEntries.text: God of the sea and father of Polyphemus. His anger makes the journey home much harder.

glossaryEntries.title: Zeus
glossaryEntries.text: King of the gods. He allows Odysseus' release from Calypso and sends the storm after Helios' cattle are harmed.

glossaryEntries.title: Hermes
glossaryEntries.text: Messenger god. He gives Odysseus protection before Circe and later carries Zeus' command to Calypso.

glossaryEntries.title: Helios
glossaryEntries.text: The Sun god whose sacred cattle must not be harmed. His anger leads to the final shipwreck.

glossaryEntries.title: Calypso
glossaryEntries.text: A powerful nymph who keeps Odysseus on Ogygia. She cares for him, but she also keeps him from home.

glossaryEntries.title: Circe
glossaryEntries.text: An enchantress on Aeaea. She begins as a danger, then becomes an uneasy helper who teaches Odysseus what comes next.

glossaryEntries.title: Eumaeus
glossaryEntries.text: The loyal swineherd who welcomes Odysseus in disguise and helps restore the household.

glossaryEntries.title: Eurycleia
glossaryEntries.text: The old nurse of Odysseus' household. She recognizes Odysseus by his scar before Penelope knows the truth.

glossaryEntries.title: Argos
glossaryEntries.text: Odysseus' old dog. Argos recognizes his master even when Odysseus is disguised.

glossaryEntries.title: Eurylochus
glossaryEntries.text: A named crewman and second-in-command figure. He is cautious at Circe's house, helps Odysseus in ritual moments, and later pushes the starving men toward the forbidden cattle.

glossaryEntries.title: Elpenor
glossaryEntries.text: The youngest and least famous of Odysseus' men. His accidental death at Circe's house gives the underworld chapter a sad, human-scale note.

glossaryEntries.title: Polites
glossaryEntries.text: A trusted, friendly crewman who encourages the scouts to approach Circe's palace. He can help make the crew feel like people rather than a crowd.

glossaryEntries.title: Perimedes
glossaryEntries.text: A named companion who helps Odysseus during serious ritual and sailing moments. Useful as a quiet, reliable sailor in the background.

glossaryEntries.title: Antinous
glossaryEntries.text: One of the boldest and cruelest suitors. He can become the main face of the suitors' threat in kid-readable scenes.

glossaryEntries.title: Eurymachus
glossaryEntries.text: A smooth-talking suitor who can seem polite while still being dangerous and selfish.

glossaryEntries.title: Mentes
glossaryEntries.text: The friendly visitor whose form Athena takes when she first gives Telemachus courage.

glossaryEntries.title: Mentor
glossaryEntries.text: An Ithacan elder whose form Athena uses while guiding Telemachus. This is where our word mentor gets its storybook power.

glossaryEntries.title: Pisistratus
glossaryEntries.text: Nestor's son, who travels with Telemachus and gives him a peer companion during the search for news.

glossaryEntries.title: Halitherses
glossaryEntries.text: An Ithacan seer who understands signs from the gods and warns that Odysseus may return.

glossaryEntries.title: Nestor
glossaryEntries.text: The old king of Pylos, famous for wisdom and memories of Troy. He welcomes Telemachus and sends him onward.

glossaryEntries.title: Menelaus
glossaryEntries.text: King of Sparta and one of the Greek leaders from Troy. He tells Telemachus that Odysseus may still be alive.

glossaryEntries.title: Helen
glossaryEntries.text: Queen of Sparta, whose story is tied to the Trojan War. She recognizes qualities of Odysseus in Telemachus.

glossaryEntries.title: Nausicaa
glossaryEntries.text: The Phaeacian princess who finds Odysseus after the storm and helps him reach safety.

glossaryEntries.title: Alcinous
glossaryEntries.text: King of the Phaeacians. He offers proper hospitality and arranges Odysseus' final voyage home.

glossaryEntries.title: Arete
glossaryEntries.text: Queen of the Phaeacians. Odysseus must approach her respectfully when asking for help.

glossaryEntries.title: Demodocus
glossaryEntries.text: The Phaeacian bard whose songs about Troy make Odysseus weep and reveal his hidden grief.

glossaryEntries.title: Laertes
glossaryEntries.text: Odysseus' father. Their reunion shows that the homecoming reaches beyond the palace.

glossaryEntries.title: Philoetius
glossaryEntries.text: A loyal cowherd who helps Odysseus, Telemachus, and Eumaeus in the final palace struggle.

glossaryEntries.title: Tiresias
glossaryEntries.text: The dead prophet who tells Odysseus how to survive the road home and warns him about Helios' cattle.

glossaryEntries.title: Anticleia
glossaryEntries.text: Odysseus' mother, whom he meets among the dead. Her scene shows the private grief inside the heroic journey.

glossaryEntries.title: Achilles
glossaryEntries.text: The great Greek warrior from Troy. In the underworld, he helps show that glory and sadness can exist together.

glossaryEntries.title: Agamemnon
glossaryEntries.text: The Greek commander from Troy. His underworld story warns Odysseus that getting home can still be dangerous.

glossaryEntries.title: Aeolus
glossaryEntries.text: The keeper of the winds, who gives Odysseus a sealed bag that should help him reach Ithaca.

glossaryEntries.title: Ino
glossaryEntries.text: A sea goddess who helps Odysseus survive Poseidon's storm by giving him a protective veil.

glossaryEntries.title: Polyphemus
glossaryEntries.text: The one-eyed Cyclops who traps Odysseus and his men. He is Poseidon's son, so Odysseus' escape has divine consequences.

glossaryEntries.title: Scylla
glossaryEntries.text: A many-headed monster on the cliffs. Odysseus chooses to pass near her because Charybdis would destroy the whole ship.

glossaryEntries.title: Charybdis
glossaryEntries.text: A terrifying whirlpool that can swallow the sea. She represents the danger of total loss.

glossaryEntries.title: Sirens
glossaryEntries.text: Enchanted singers whose beautiful song pulls sailors toward destruction.

glossaryEntries.title: Odysseus' Crew
glossaryEntries.text: The sailors are not just background. Their hunger, fear, mistrust, and longing for home drive many of the journey's hardest choices.

glossaryEntries.title: The Suitors
glossaryEntries.text: The men crowding Odysseus' palace and pressuring Penelope. Antinous and Eurymachus are the clearest named faces of this threat.

glossaryEntries.title: The Cicones
glossaryEntries.text: The people of Ismarus, whose counterattack teaches Odysseus' crew that the habits of war can follow them into the journey home.

glossaryEntries.title: Lotus-Eaters
glossaryEntries.text: A gentle but dangerous people whose lotus flowers make visitors forget home and the desire to leave.

glossaryEntries.title: Laestrygonians
glossaryEntries.text: Terrifying giants who trap most of Odysseus' fleet in their harbor. Their scene changes the journey from twelve ships to one.

glossaryEntries.title: Ithaca
glossaryEntries.text: Odysseus' island home. The journey is not finished until the house and kingdom are made whole again.

glossaryEntries.title: Pylos
glossaryEntries.text: The kingdom of Nestor, where Telemachus first enters the world of older heroes and proper hospitality.

glossaryEntries.title: Sparta
glossaryEntries.text: The palace of Menelaus and Helen, where Telemachus hears that Odysseus may still be alive.

glossaryEntries.title: Troy
glossaryEntries.text: The war city Odysseus leaves behind at the beginning of the journey. Its shadow follows the crew into the first chapters.

glossaryEntries.title: Land of the Cicones
glossaryEntries.text: The first stop after Troy, often connected with Ismarus and Thrace in parent map notes.

glossaryEntries.title: Ithaca Palace
glossaryEntries.text: The center of Odysseus' household, where Penelope waits, the suitors waste the family's goods, and the homecoming is finally tested.

glossaryEntries.title: Ogygia
glossaryEntries.text: Calypso's beautiful island, where Odysseus is safe but unable to return home for many years.

glossaryEntries.title: Scheria Shore
glossaryEntries.text: The shore where Odysseus arrives with nothing after Poseidon's storm destroys his raft.

glossaryEntries.title: Phaeacian Palace
glossaryEntries.text: The generous court of Alcinous and Arete, where Odysseus receives hospitality and earns the voyage home.

glossaryEntries.title: Land of the Lotus-Eaters
glossaryEntries.text: A soft, dreamy place where the danger is forgetting home rather than being attacked.

glossaryEntries.title: Island of the Cyclopes
glossaryEntries.text: The rough island where Odysseus enters Polyphemus' cave and learns how dangerous bad hospitality can be.

glossaryEntries.title: Aeolia
glossaryEntries.text: The island of Aeolus, where a magical gift brings Odysseus almost home before mistrust blows the ships away.

glossaryEntries.title: Land of the Laestrygonians
glossaryEntries.text: A cliff-ringed harbor where most of Odysseus' fleet is trapped and destroyed.

glossaryEntries.title: Aeaea
glossaryEntries.text: Circe's island, first a place of enchantment and danger, then a strange pause where Odysseus receives guidance.

glossaryEntries.title: The Underworld
glossaryEntries.text: A spiritual place beyond normal geography, where Odysseus speaks with the dead and learns what the journey has cost.

glossaryEntries.title: The Sirens' Coast
glossaryEntries.text: The dangerous coastline where Odysseus hears the Sirens while his crew rows safely past with their ears sealed.

glossaryEntries.title: Scylla and Charybdis
glossaryEntries.text: The narrow passage between monster and whirlpool, often connected in parent notes with the Strait of Messina.

glossaryEntries.title: Thrinacia
glossaryEntries.text: The island of Helios' sacred cattle, where hunger, warning, and disobedience lead to the final shipwreck.

glossaryEntries.title: The Last Shipwreck
glossaryEntries.text: A route node rather than a fixed place: Zeus' storm destroys the last ship, and Odysseus is left alone.

glossaryEntries.title: Eumaeus' Hut
glossaryEntries.text: The humble shelter where Odysseus first tests loyalty at home and where Telemachus recognizes his father.

glossaryEntries.title: Ithaca Countryside
glossaryEntries.text: The countryside around Laertes' farm, where the final threat of revenge is stopped and peace returns.

glossaryEntries.title: Hospitality
glossaryEntries.text: The ancient rule that guests and strangers should be treated with respect. Good hosts and bad hosts shape the whole story.

locationNodes.label: Troy
locationNodes.parentGeographyNote: Ancient Troy is commonly associated with Hisarlik in modern Turkey.

locationNodes.label: Land of the Cicones
locationNodes.parentGeographyNote: Often associated with Ismarus and Thrace; useful as an early route stop.

locationNodes.label: Ithaca Palace
locationNodes.parentGeographyNote: Modern Ithaca is real, though ancient Ithaca debates exist.

locationNodes.label: Pylos
locationNodes.parentGeographyNote: Usually associated with Pylos in the southwest Peloponnese.

locationNodes.label: Sparta
locationNodes.parentGeographyNote: A real ancient region and city-state in the Peloponnese.

locationNodes.label: Ogygia
locationNodes.parentGeographyNote: Many proposals exist; best kept mythic in the base map.

locationNodes.label: Scheria Shore
locationNodes.parentGeographyNote: Sometimes linked with Corfu, but uncertain.

locationNodes.label: Phaeacian Palace
locationNodes.parentGeographyNote: A mythic court of ideal hospitality.

locationNodes.label: Land of the Lotus-Eaters
locationNodes.parentGeographyNote: Ancient and modern identifications vary widely.

locationNodes.label: Island of the Cyclopes
locationNodes.parentGeographyNote: Keep mythic unless later map mode explores theories.

locationNodes.label: Aeolia
locationNodes.parentGeographyNote: Often impossible to place with certainty.

locationNodes.label: Land of the Laestrygonians
locationNodes.parentGeographyNote: Some later identifications exist, but mythic works best.

locationNodes.label: Aeaea
locationNodes.parentGeographyNote: Later traditions connect it with Italy, but uncertain.

locationNodes.label: The Underworld
locationNodes.parentGeographyNote: Not a normal geographic stop.

locationNodes.label: The Sirens
locationNodes.parentGeographyNote: Later traditions place the Sirens near southern Italy, but the base map should keep this interpretive.

locationNodes.label: Scylla and Charybdis
locationNodes.parentGeographyNote: Often associated with the Strait of Messina.

locationNodes.label: Thrinacia
locationNodes.parentGeographyNote: Often associated by later readers with Sicily.

locationNodes.label: The Last Shipwreck
locationNodes.parentGeographyNote: A connective sea node rather than a fixed location.
